newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Competition to hit Japan investment funds.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Competition to hit Japan investment funds.

text.p: Sweeping "Big Bang" financial reforms mean Japan's fund management firms will have to face something they've never dealt with before -- cut-throat competition.
Japanese investment trust funds, like mutual funds in the United States, are investment vehicles that pool money from a wide range of individuals and invest it in stocks and bonds.

"The Big Bang will change Japan's trust fund market into an international place, where competitiveness is the key to survival," said Kenji Iguchi, general manager at Asahi Investment Trust Management Co Ltd.
"The better a fund performs, the greater the flow of money into it," he added.
In the past, the success of a fund depended largely on the sales power of the affiliated brokerage selling it.
Because of their reluctance to invest in risk-contained assets, the share of cash and bank deposits held by Japanese individuals are relatively high.

Sumitomo Bank Ltd estimated that the amount of investment trust funds held by individuals would reach 55 trillion yen ($478 billion) of the total individual assets of about 1,406 ($12.23 trillion) by the end of 2000.
It is expected to soar to 107 trillion yen ($930 billion) of a total of 1,698 trillion yen ($14.76 trillion) by 2005.

"There's a possibility of risk-contained assets (stocks, foreign bonds and trust funds) increasing to a half of total assets over the next decade," said Hiroshi Yamamura, director of the economic research department at NLI Research Institute.
Yamamura, however, said there was still a question as to whether investment trusts will become attractive to the elderly, who hold their savings in cash and deposits.
FOREIGN COMPANIES EYE JAPANESE ASSETS

The broad financial reforms, expected to be implemented by 2001 by the latest, will allow foreign companies with their competitive investment skills to grab a bigger slice of Japan's huge individual investment pie.
Companies such as Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse have apparently already taken the lead by accumulating management funds from individuals and Japan's big pension fund bodies.
Goldman Sachs Investment Trust Management Co Ltd, an affiliate of Goldman Sachs Group LP, has made remarkable strides since it launched its first investment fund just one year ago.
By the end of April, it had collected 420 billion yen in individual investment funds, the largest amount of the 15 foreign investment trust firms operating in Japan.
Goldman has attracted many individual investors by using its global research and management networks to invest in global stocks, bonds and currencies.
"We hope to make our funds products which function as long-term savings," said an official at Goldman Sachs Investment.

Toshio Fukuda, president and managing director at Credit Suisse Investment Trust Management Co Ltd, an affiliate firm of Credit Suisse Group said: "Without the Big Bang, we would be a niche player in Tokyo, but the financial reforms will alter the existing rules and investor behaviour and hopefully give us a chance to become a major player.
"It may be extreme to say it, but there haven't really been any long-term investors or core investment products in Japan's investment trust fund market," Fukuda said.

He added that the current fixed pension fund system faces limits due to money shortages and the ageing society and thus a partial shift into a U.S.-style 401K defined contribution pension plan was needed.
"Japanese individuals would then think seriously about who manages their retirement funds or saving assets for the first time," he added.

In Japan, the benefits that an employee will receive on retirement are set beforehand. The 401K plan allows people to make annual pre-tax contributions, with the benefits from the plan depending on how well those contributions are invested.
STOCK FUND COLLAPSE

But individual Japanese investors still have a negative impression of domestic investment trust funds, partly because stock funds they invested heavily in during the late 1980s economic "bubble" of inflated asset prices turned out to be disastrous.
The key Tokyo stock index is trading at just over half of its December 1989 peak of about 38,900 points.
"The impression of investment trust funds in Japan are quite bad," said Kumi Fujisawa, an analyst of AFIS, a fund evaluation company.
A series of recent financial scandals has also sown distrust of Japanese brokers and fund management companies.

Nikko Securities Investment Trust and Management, an affiliate of Nikko Securities Co Ltd, admitted in May that it had conducted illegal dealings in 1994 involving trades in foreign bonds at prices above their market prices.

Earlier this month, advisory panels to the Ministry of Finance unveiled recommendations of its planned financial reforms, which urged an introduction of privately placed trust funds. To give consumers a wider choice of funds, the panels also urged that commercial banks be allowed to sell the funds.

Japan's Investment Trusts Association decided in April that it would provide data on such things as net asset value per unit and net asset outstanding of each fund, to fund evaluation companies so they in turn can provide comparisons to investors.
Fund evaluation firms are well-established in the United States but did not exist in Japan until recently.
"We believe that changes always begin on the consumer side rather than the production or sales side," said Fujisawa. "We hope to use this principle for investment trust funds, too."
